ANNEX to GB decision no CAJU-GB-Writ proc 2025-09 WPB 2026-2027
WORK PROGRAMME and BUDGET
2026-2027
In accordance with the Council Regulation (EU) No Council Regulation (EU) No 2085/2021 of 19
November 2021 establishing the Joint Undertakings under Horizon Europe and with Article 31 of the
Financial Rules of the Clean Aviation JU.
The Work Programme and Budget 2026-2027 is made publicly available after its adoption by the
Governing Board.
The ‘Work Programme and Budget 2026-2027’ refers specifically to the Clean Aviation Joint
Undertaking (CAJU) Work Programme and is distinct from the Horizon Europe (HE) Work
Programme. While CAJU operates within the Horizon Europe, its Work Programme is an
independent document adopted by the CAJU Governing Board in accordance with Council
Regulation (EU) 2021/2085 establishing the Joint Undertakings.
1

1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Mission statement of the Clean Aviation Joint Undertaking
The Clean Aviation Joint Undertaking (CAJU) will develop disruptive new aircraft technologies to
support the European Green Deal and achieve climate neutrality by 2050. These technologies will
deliver net greenhouse gas (GHG) reductions of no less than 30%, compared to the 2020 state-of-the-
art. The technological and industrial readiness will allow the deployment of new aircraft incorporating
these technologies no later than 2035, enabling 75% of the world’s civil aviation fleet to be replaced by
2050. The aircraft developed will enable net CO reductions of up to 90% when combined with the
2
effect of sustainable ‘drop-in’ fuels, or zero CO emissions in flight when using hydrogen as an energy
2
source.
Clean Aviation’s aeronautics-related research and innovation activities, focusing on breakthrough
technology initiatives, will contribute to the global sustainable competitiveness of the European
aviation industry. Our efforts will ensure that aviation remains a safe and secure, reliable, cost-effective
and efficient means of passenger and freight transportation while successfully transitioning to climate
neutrality. European aviation research and innovation capacity will be strengthened through this
partnership, enabling new and ambitious global standards to be set.
1.2 Background and link with the Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda
Europe needs to accelerate and enhance its efforts to achieve the ambitious goals set out in the Paris
Agreement. The European Green Deal is a cornerstone policy of the European Union. It sets out the
path to achieving Europe’s leading contribution. It includes the first European Climate Law, enshrining
the 2050 climate neutrality objective in legislation. At the same time, the Industrial Strategy for Europe
lays out in clear terms the importance of industrial leadership in making the transformation to a green
and digital Europe fit for the future.
The European aviation sector will need to contribute to these priorities. This will involve
transformational change to aircraft entering into operation, including their propulsion, on-board
systems and structures, and including compatibility with new fuel or energy sources used. Disruptive
innovation to enable this transformation will need to be coupled with appropriate measures and
policies that allow for the timely introduction of infrastructures, the required ramp-up in availability of
renewable energy and the production of hydrogen and ‘sustainable aviation fuels’. The common
challenge is to lead the way towards a climate neutral aviation system and set new global standards for
safe, reliable, affordable, and clean air transport.
The journey to a climate-neutral aviation system is well beyond the capability and investment capacity
of the private sector alone. Equally, no single country in Europe has the financial, technological and
industrial capability to effect the transformation. The European additionality is evident. The
institutionalised European Partnership for Clean Aviation under Horizon Europe (i.e. the Clean Aviation
Joint Undertaking) constitutes the only approach that can pull together the required resources and
commitments and adequately reduce the industrial risk for transformative research and innovation
[R&I].
This approach secures the long-term industrial commitments needed for long innovation cycles. It
ensures that research activities of industry are aligned with the Union’s policy priorities. It contributes
4

to building Europe’s leadership in innovation and technology and deliver jobs and economic growth
throughout the transition to a climate-neutral Europe by 2050. The approach can offer future
generations the promise of continued, affordable and equal access to air travel, with all its social and
economic benefits, and contribute to the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals.
The Clean Aviation Joint Undertaking’s Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda [SRIA], updated in
September 2024, sets out the way to achieve the overall vision, in terms of timescales and magnitude
of impact. The Clean Aviation trajectory defines two clear horizons towards climate neutrality by
2050.The SRIA was updated are to:
• ensure that the programme’s vision and overall ambition remain aligned to the programme’s
objectives as set out in the Council Regulation (EU) 2021/2085 with the availability of 1.7 billion
€ in EU funding;
• define the programme’s Phase 2 agenda (2025-2030) to integrate and demonstrate disruptive
technological innovations around four targeted European aircraft concepts and one scalable
demonstration concept. These concepts serve as reference aircraft concepts targeting the
expected impact as defined in the article 57.2 of the Council Regulation for the integration and
demonstration of impactful technological innovations within Clean Aviation, as well as for
relevant innovations supported by other EU, national, and regional programmes;
• refine the programme’s Phase 2 agenda based on the performed activities and available critical
results from projects funded by the partnership since its launch, i.e. in Phase 1 (2022-2026) of
the programme;
• integrate, at the core of the SRIA, the cooperation based on synergies with other parts and
partnerships of Horizon Europe and other EU, National and Regional programmes to maximise
impact on the partnership’s objectives as set out in the Council Regulation (EU) 2021/20851
and the SRIA.
1.3. Strategy for the implementation of the programme
The programme’s high-level objectives (HLO) as set in the Council Regulation (EU) 2021/2085 have been
laid down in the vision and the overall ambition of the SRIA (see previous chapter). These have
subsequently been translated into an executable Technology Roadmap that has served as the basis for
the Work Programme, with topics including technical requirements, critical milestones, expected
decision gates, and targets that will allow for the selection and execution of clearly defined research
actions, contributing to the achievement of the programme’s HLO.
The Clean Aviation programme is built on three key thrusts, each with targeted R&I and demonstration
efforts driving the energy efficiency and the emissions reduction of future aircraft. Each thrust will
develop technologies and enablers, leverage essential knowledge and capabilities, and de-risk the
identified technologies and solutions, where further maturation, validation and demonstration is
required to maximise impact (see chapter 2.2.2 “Scientific priorities, challenges and expected impact”):
• Disruptive technologies for ultra-efficient REgional Aircraft (REG)
• Disruptive technologies for ultra-efficient Short/short-Medium Range aircraft (SMR)
• Disruptive technologies to enable hydrogen-powered aircraft (HPA)
The implementation of the Clean Aviation work programme is divided into two phases:
• The first phase of the programme (Phase 1: 2022–2026 – technology maturation) is dedicated
to identifying high-potential disruptive aircraft concept(s) by assessing a broad set of
potentially relevant configurations. This includes the development and maturation of the

• The second phase of the programme (Phase 2: 2025-2030 – integration and demonstration),
will focus on the integration and demonstration of technologies around the Clean Aviation
targeted aircraft concepts which are expected to be powered either by Sustainable Aviation
fuel (SAF) or hydrogen, combined with electric hybridisation. These concepts have the potential
to reduce CO emissions by no less than 30% and to meet a technology readiness level (up to
2
TRL6) to support the launch of new products and services for an Entry into Service (EIS) in 2035
for the next generation of aircraft, in order to achieve the emission reduction impact. Key
elements of this phase will be large-scale integrated aircraft component/system tests and
large-scale flying demonstrator platforms to validate and demonstrate the performance of the
key technologies and the targeted aircraft at realistic sizes and operational conditions.
The CAJU will identify those technical solutions with the highest impact in terms of climate, combined
with the best chance of evolving into sustainable product and service innovations, including the
demonstration of new ambitious technology solutions and climate-neutral aircraft concepts, via
competitive calls for proposals, open to all interested stakeholders willing to commit, contribute and
collaborate in the partnership. This approach will allow for long-term allocation of budget through
multi-annual grant agreements in line with the open calls and the CAJU financial rules on multi-annual
commitments. The CAJU’s Work Programme will identify and govern the calls, topics and related R&I
actions.
The appropriate number of calls will be defined in the light of the content of the SRIA (up to three calls
on a yearly basis over the period 2025-2027) based on critical results from Phase 1 and, proposed
approach throughout Phase 2, to accelerate the maturation, integration and demonstration of the most
promising breakthrough innovations coherently with private members’ market strategies and in
particular with the ambition to target entry into service of such innovations by 2035.
The CAJU will also build on important contributions arising from cooperation based on synergies with
other parts and partnerships of Horizon Europe and other EU, National and Regional programmes, as
well as from earlier research carried out under previous Framework Programmes on R&I (such as under
the Clean Sky and Clean Sky 2 programmes) and on the experience gained from managing these.

2 WORK PROGRAMME 2026-2027
2.1 Executive summary
The present Work Programme and its accompanying Budget Plan for 2026–2027 set out the main
highlights and scientific priorities of the technical, administrative, and financial activities to be
implemented under the Clean Aviation Joint Undertaking (CAJU). This document defines the scope of
actions to be undertaken during the period 2026–2027, ensuring continued alignment with the
overarching objective of achieving climate neutrality for aviation by 2050, in line with the European
Green Deal.
The joint commitment of the public and private members, together with the Programme Office, will
remain essential to ensure the successful delivery of this ambitious research and innovation
programme. Over the period 2026–2027, the CAJU will focus its efforts on the execution of Phase 1 and
the consolidation and advancement of Phase 2, building on the achievements and lessons learned from
the implementation of the 2022–2025 Work Programmes.
The 2026–2027 Work Programme covers:
• the execution of Phase 1, through the implementation, monitoring and assessment of
Innovation Actions (IAs) and Coordination and Support Actions (CSAs) selected from the Calls
for Proposals launched under the 2022 and 2023 Work Programmes, addressing the activities
required in the three thrusts — Short-Medium Range (SMR), Hybrid-Electric Regional (HER) and
Hydrogen-Powered Aircraft (HPA);
• the execution of Phase 2, through the implementation, monitoring and assessment of
Innovation Actions (IAs) and Research Actions (RAs) selected from the third Call for Proposals
launched under the 2024–2025 Work Programme;
• the preparation and launch of new Calls for Proposals under Phase 2 in 2026 and 2027, followed
by the evaluation and selection of proposals for funding.
The proposed strategy foresees the launch of one call per year, in early 2026 (Call 4) and early 2027
(Call 5), as part of the total funding envelope of approximately €930 million available for Phase 2. These
calls will focus on the integration and demonstration of technological innovations around the targeted
aircraft concepts set out in the Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda (SRIA).
Both calls will include Fast Track Activities (FTAs) designed to provide greater flexibility, create
additional opportunities for Research and Technology Organisations (RTOs), academia and SMEs, and
accelerate the maturation of complementary and alternative technologies. While Call 4 will target
smaller projects in terms of budget and technical complexity, Call 5 will mainly address large-scale
demonstration activities contributing to the market uptake of disruptive technologies and innovative
solutions.
The preparation of these calls will be informed by progress achieved in Phase 1 and will be contingent
upon projects achieving at least Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 by their completion. The decision
to launch subsequent activities will follow the decision gates indicated in the Gantt charts of the
targeted aircraft concepts and will depend on the confirmation of maturity levels achieved.
In addition to grant-based activities, the CAJU will launch operational Calls for Tenders to procure
studies and services supporting its statutory tasks and strategic objectives. These tenders will
contribute to assessing the environmental, economic and societal impact of the technologies
developed under Clean Aviation, identifying barriers to early market adoption, and strengthening
synergies with other Horizon Europe initiatives and EU programmes.
7

In particular, a tender planned for 2026 will commission an independent study to assess the expected
programme impact, forecast the uptake of technologies towards climate neutrality, and provide
recommendations to address remaining challenges and ensure the successful entry into service of low-
emission aircraft by 2035.
Strengthening cooperation and synergies will remain at the core of Clean Aviation’s strategy to
maximise scientific, socio-economic and environmental impact. Collaboration with the European Union
Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) formalised through the Memorandum of Cooperation signed in 2022 will
continue to focus on de-risking and demonstrating the feasibility of new aircraft concepts, developing
novel certification methods, and evolving regulatory frameworks in coordination with international
bodies such as ICAO.
In parallel, CAJU will pursue closer collaboration with other Horizon Europe Joint Undertakings,
including the Clean Hydrogen JU, SESAR 3 JU and BATT4EU, to ensure coherent progress across
interlinked technology areas such as hydrogen propulsion, air traffic management and advanced
batteries. Synergies will also be developed with the Made in Europe and Chips Joint Undertakings, as
well as relevant activities under Cluster 5 of Horizon Europe.
At national and regional level, the CAJU will intensify the implementation of its Action Plan on Synergies
with European Aeronautics Regions and Member States, developed in cooperation with the European
Commission’s DG Research and Innovation (“Clean Planet” Directorate). This plan aims to accelerate
the maturation and demonstration of low-emission aircraft technologies, leveraging complementary
investments from regional and national funding instruments such as Cohesion Policy Funds (ERDF) and
National Recovery and Resilience Plans (NRRPs).
The CAJU will build on the existing Memoranda of Cooperation (MoCs) established with Andalucía,
Occitanie, Hamburg, Piemonte, Campania, and Portugal, while expanding its network through an 18-
month technical assistance tender launched in late 2025 to further develop regional cooperation in
support of the Clean Aviation roadmap.
Internationally, CAJU will continue to play an active role in the Alliance for Zero Emission Aviation
(AZEA), focusing on infrastructure, certification and operational requirements for hydrogen and electric
aircraft, while seeking synergies with other EU initiatives such as the European Innovation Fund.
Communication and outreach activities will remain a strategic pillar in positioning Clean Aviation as
Europe’s leading hub for research and innovation in sustainable and competitive aviation. The
Communication Strategy 2026–2027 is structured around five pillars: Awareness, Engagement,
Influence, Progress, and Branding designed to enhance visibility, strengthen stakeholder engagement
and consolidate the CAJU’s reputation as a thought leader in the field of sustainable aviation. High-
profile initiatives, including the Clean Aviation Annual Forum 2026, participation in major international
airshows, will ensure the programme’s achievements are effectively communicated to political,
technical and societal audiences across Europe.
Throughout this period, the CAJU will continue to apply the principles of sound financial management,
transparency and accountability in line with its Financial Rules and the Single Basic Act. Administrative
and operational processes will be further digitalised through the deployment of new ICT systems, while
cooperation with other Joint Undertakings under the Back Office Arrangements (BOA) will continue to
deliver efficiencies and ensure harmonised best practices.
8

Overall, this Work Programme and Budget 2026–2027 provides the roadmap for the next phase in
delivering on Clean Aviation’s mission: transforming Europe’s world-class aeronautical research into
disruptive, demonstrable technologies, accelerating progress towards net-zero aviation, and
consolidating Europe’s leadership in sustainable air transport.
2.2 Message from the Executive Director
Dear Readers,
Clean Aviation continues to advance disruptive technological innovations for the next generation of low-
emission and climate neutral aircraft, accelerating Europe’s pathway towards sustainable aviation and
strengthening European industrial leadership and global competitiveness in the field of aviation.
As Phase 2 of our programme began in early 2025, we launched Call 3, a major milestone in our journey.
For the first time, we introduced Fast Track Activities (FTA) – a mechanism designed to de-risk alternative
or complementary technical solutions and accelerate their integration. With this, we aimed to attract
start-ups, universities, and research centres, whose ability to think outside the box is critical to driving
disruptive innovation. We also piloted the PitchAthlon & Connect event, giving applicants a unique
platform to pitch their expertise and demonstrate their potential contributions to Call 3 topics. These
new instruments have strengthened collaboration and inclusiveness within our ecosystem. Call 3 has
therefore both expanded our portfolio and marked a significant evolution in the way Clean Aviation
supports innovation.
At the heart of this progress remain our projects – the backbone of our impact. By accelerating the
maturation of breakthrough solutions and preparing for integrated demonstrations that will raise
technology readiness levels by 2030, we are laying the foundations for a cleaner and more competitive
future. With the new Call 3 projects set to launch by the end of 2025, our portfolio will comprise around
40 projects, each contributing to our shared vision.
Our Impact Assessment Report (IAR), presented to the Governing Board mid-year, confirms that the
programme is firmly on track to meet its high-level objectives. The evidence demonstrates clear progress
in accelerating technology development, mobilising stakeholders across industry and research, and
keeping alignment with Europe’s climate neutrality goals. The IAR also points to the growing visibility
and recognition of Clean Aviation across Europe, reflecting both the scale of our ambition and the
credibility of our delivery.
We continue to deepen our synergies with Member States and European regions. Notable examples
include Memoranda of Cooperation with Andalucía and Portugal, both representing tangible steps in
aligning regional and national priorities with European ambitions. These initiatives highlight the
importance of pooling resources and fostering joint action at all levels to achieve shared objectives.
Looking ahead, preparations for Calls 4 and 5 are already well under way. These calls will further expand
our portfolio and consolidate the technological pathways defined in our Strategic Research & Innovation
Agenda (SRIA), ensuring continued momentum and delivery on our ambitious agenda.
Looking further into the future, the European Commission has raised its ambition and taken a significant
step in its proposal for the MFF 2028–2034. Beyond proposing a substantial increase for Horizon Europe
R&I budget, it has announced a close connection with the proposed European Competitiveness Fund
(ECF). In this context and following the elaboration of the Aviation R&I Strategy (ARIS) by over 100
aviation stakeholders, a “Clean Aviation moonshot” project for a Smart and Clean Aviation Partnership

with industry has been proposed. This recognition underscores the strategic importance of the European
aviation sector and of Clean Aviation in delivering transformative technologies and strengthening
Europe’s long-term industrial leadership and competitiveness.
I would also like to acknowledge recent changes within our Governing Board. Joanna Drake, Deputy
Director-General at the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Research and Innovation, has
taken over ad interim as Chair, succeeding Rosalinde van der Vlies, Director in the Commission’s
Directorate for Just Transition, Consumers, Efficiency and Innovation, to whom we owe our gratitude,
as a strong supporter of the Joint Undertaking. We also warmly thank Sabine Klauke (Airbus) for her

Rémi Maillard (Airbus), who will continue her legacy of strong commitment and guidance.
Together with our partners and stakeholders, Clean Aviation will continue to drive innovation,
sustainability, and competitiveness. The Work Programme 2026–2027 reflects not only our collective

European aviation sector.
Axel Krein
Executive Director
2.3 Operational activities of the Clean Aviation JU
2.3.1 Scientific priorities, challenges and expected impact
The mission of the Clean Aviation Partnership is to develop disruptive new aircraft technologies to pave
the way towards the EU’s ambition of climate neutrality by 2050. Since its establishment in November
2021, the Joint Undertaking has launched large-size, industry-led projects that are developing novel
concepts for the next-generation of low-emissions commercial aircraft; investigating various disruptive
aircraft technological innovations options powered either by Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF) or
hydrogen, combined with electric hybridization; and performing trade studies to assess various aircraft
configurations incorporating the most promising technology options aiming at reducing greenhouse
gas (GHG) emissions by no less than 30% at aircraft level by 2030, compared to 2020 state-of-the-art,
while enabling zero CO emissions in flight when using hydrogen as energy source, or up to 90% net-
2
CO -emission reduction when being combined with the effect of Sustainable Aviation Fuels.
2
The following specific high-level objectives are defined in the Council Regulation 2021/2085 as adopted
by the European Council on 19 November 2021:
(a) to integrate and demonstrate disruptive aircraft technological innovations able to decrease net
emissions of greenhouse gases by no less than 30% by 2030, compared to 2020 state-of-the-art
technology, while paving the ground towards climate-neutral aviation by 2050;
(b) to ensure that the technological and the potential industrial readiness of innovations can support
the launch of disruptive new products and services by 2035, with the aim of contributing to the
replacement of 75% of the operating fleet by 2050 and developing an innovative, reliable, safe and
cost-effective European aviation system that is able to meet the objective of climate neutrality at
the latest by 2050;
(c) to expand and foster integration of the climate-neutral aviation research and innovation value
chains, including academia, research organisations, industry and SMEs, also by benefiting from
10

exploiting synergies with other national and European related programmes and by supporting the
uptake of industry-related skills across the value chain.
The Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda [SRIA] revised and published in September 2024 defines
the aircraft concepts vision serving as references to mature and integrate aircraft innovative
technologies with the aim to deliver impact as defined in the article 57.2 of the council regulation. It
incorporates changes to align with the budget allocation and availability of €1.7 billion in EU funding
while maintaining the ambition unchanged, to revise the strategic planning to align with the effective
date of launch of the programme’s operations in 2021 and to revise its strategic content with activities
launched through the open calls in Phase 1 of the programme.
As part of the programme’s Phase 1 (2022-2026), 28 Clean Aviation projects have started with more
than €800 million in European Union funding through Horizon Europe. This public-side support is
complemented and leveraged by a declared private-side in-kind contributions amounting to a total
research effort of €2 billion, confirming a strong commitment by the European aviation ecosystem
(industry, supply chain research organization, academia and SMEs) through their membership and
participation to the Joint Undertaking to achieving the programme objectives and contributing to
transforming European aviation towards a sustainable and more competitive system.
SRIA provides the vision for the 2nd Phase of the programme and outlines aircraft technological
innovations proposed around four (4) aircraft concepts: one concept is linked to the ultra-efficient SMR
thrust, one concept to the ultra-efficient Regional thrust, and two concepts for the Hydrogen-Powered
Aircraft thrust.
As part of the programme’s Phase 2 (2026-2030), the projects selected as part of Call 3 are expected
to start in early 2026 upon successful completion of the grant agreement preparation. These projects
will focus on the integration and demonstration of technologies around the Clean Aviation targeted
aircraft concepts on SMR and REG and, via the Fast Track Areas (FTAs) mechanism, on de-risking
alternative or complementary technical solutions, enlarging the breadth of competencies including
from universities, research centres, and SMEs.
The technological content and the demonstration strategies, proposed in each of the three thrusts for
the second phase of Clean Aviation, will have to refer to one or more of the aircraft concepts. These
aircraft concepts, addressing the SMR and Regional segments (with some spill over benefits to long
range segment), offer the best potential to decrease net-greenhouse gas emissions by no less than 30%
at aircraft level and to ensure that the technological industrial readiness of innovations achieved at
completion (up to TRL 6 by 2030) can support the launch of disruptive new products and services for
an entry into service by 2035.
These aircraft concepts will serve as reference exploitation route guidelines for the innovative
technologies being developed in the first phase of Clean Aviation, as well as for technologies that could
emerge from synergies with other EU instruments (e.g. SESAR, Clean Hydrogen, BATT4EU etc.) or
National Programmes.

Three key thrusts for the R&I efforts have been identified to drive the energy efficiency and the
emissions reductions of future aircraft, in line with the European aircraft concepts described above

Ultra-efficient Short and Medium-Range (SMR) aircraft architectures – to address the short- medium

By the end of 2025, Clean Aviation awarded funding to 28 projects across its first and second calls for
proposals (see ‘Overview of Phase 1 Projects’ below), with 4 projects already closing in 2025 (ECARE,
CLAIM, FASTER-H2 and HECATE). The 24 on-going Phase 1 projects are running their full course, with
several grants amended and extended into 2026 to reflect the 2024 SRIA update and adjustments in

milestones for each of these projects and activities expected to be achieved by the end of Phase 1.
Overview of Phase 1 Projects
2.3.1.1. Disruptive technologies for ultra-efficient Regional Aircraft (REG)
Greater attention to environmental concerns, along with stringent regulations and higher market
demand are changing regional air mobility – and specifically for missions between 463 km and 926 km.
Currently, regional aviation plays a major role in air mobility. Thanks to their widespread distribution,
both propeller and jet regional aircraft-operated routes and connections now account for over 12% of
world ASK (available seat kilometres). Regional aircraft currently serve roughly 38% of world city pairs and
perform about 40% of the total departures and around 36% of the total flown hours. In terms of regional
connectivity, 36% of existing airports are relying exclusively on regional turboprop-operated services.
The ambition for propeller regional aircraft is to replace regional jets, which are more expensive in
14

operations and produce more emissions; in particular on shorter regional or feeder routes, where
propeller regional aircraft can maintain a reliable and effective network with only a very small-time
penalty.
By the mid-2030s, innovations and technologies to improve affordability, match customer expectations,
and enable the optimisation of propulsion systems for different fuel types and airframe characteristics
will reach higher levels of maturity and become available for regional air transport.
The Ultra-Efficient Regional Aircraft (UERA) concept, with a capacity of 50 to 100 seats, is expected to
be among the earliest applications of hybrid-electric propulsion technologies in the scheduled air
transport system. This concept will come with solutions to reduce the environmental footprint, and
provisions to maximise fleet penetration and impact, thus paving the way for affordable sustainable
aviation.
Smaller air vehicles, such as commuters and rotorcraft operating on shorter or thinner routes will also
benefit from electric propulsion solutions tested on regional aircraft testbeds. These vehicles will use
similar power modules, with different approaches to air vehicle integration.
The ultra-efficient regional thrust (REG) will demonstrate at high TRL a set of innovative and disruptive
technologies ready for entry into service by 2035. The UERA concept will incorporate product-viable
solutions that take into account technology, integration, industrialisation, infrastructure, and certification
aspects. The aircraft will include hybrid-electric propulsion based on batteries, supported by 100% drop-
in sustainable fuels for the thermal power source, to reach at least 30% lower CO emissions (without
2
SAF net-CO contribution) from disruptive technology solutions, while being fully compliant with ICAO
2
noise rules and incorporating solutions to improve impact and fleet penetration. The parameters linked
to non-CO effects will be monitored and reported.
2
Careful aircraft integration of selected technologies is required to achieve both the sustainability and
fleet replacement targets of Clean Aviation.
In the first phase of the programme (2022- 2026) the technology building blocks (propulsion, airframe,
and system technologies) are being matures and different integration options are being studied to
assess their potential and integration perspectives; this has enabled the identification of the most
promising architectures. Various propulsion and aircraft configurations were initially assessed in trade-
offs. A comparison of various propulsion configurations is carried out, e.g. distributed propulsion and/or
parallel/serial propulsion, including transfer of electric power to the engine shaft. Various levels of
hybridisation and different primary energy sources are explored including a thermal engine, batteries
or potentially fuel cells (see the Hydrogen Powered Aircraft section below) as part of the hybrid-electric
configuration.
Clean Aviation projects selected in the first phase of the programme and contributing to the REG thrust
include HE-ART and AMBER, developing Multi-Mega Watt hybrid electric power trains and related
techno-bricks; TheMa4HERA, developing thermal management solutions; HECATE, developing electric
distribution solutions; HERWINGT, developing wing technologies and architecture; HERFUSE,
developing fuselage and empennage technologies integrating hybrid-electric systems and energy
storage; and ODE4HERA, developing an Open Digital Platform. Finally, HERA is developing the aircraft
architecture for the several aircraft concepts, and performs the aircraft-level integration of
technologies developed by the other selected projects.
As a result of these phase 1 studies and in line with the updated Clean Aviation SRIA, the battery-based
UERA concept was proposed as the baseline concept for the Regional thrust in phase 2, as a solution
compatible with a 2035 EIS. More disruptive options (e.g. based on H2 Fuel Cell electrical power) are
considered by phase 1 projects for longer-term application beyond 2035.

2.3.1.3. Disruptive technologies to enable hydrogen-powered aircraft (HPA)
Hydrogen is a promising energy vector for the future, as its usage in a combustion chamber or fuel cell
results in zero-carbon emissions. If produced with low- or zero-carbon electricity, hydrogen has the
potential to strongly reduce the environmental impact of transport systems, including aviation.
Hydrogen has several key advantages for aviation application; it allows for the elimination of CO
2
emissions in flight, and along the entire life-cycle if produced by carbon-free energy sources. In terms
of non-CO emissions, the use of hydrogen in a combustion or fuel cell engine can lead to different
2
emissions. Its usage in fuel cells allows for zero NOx and particulate emission. When hydrogen is burnt
in a turbine engine, very low particle emissions can be expected, as well as reduced NOx emissions
(provided that the combustion system is optimised). Nevertheless, both hydrogen fuel cell and
hydrogen combustion propulsion systems will result in an increase in water emissions, which could
increase the risk of persistent contrails formation and hence can have an impact on the environment.
To enable the use of hydrogen to propel an aircraft, several technological advancements need to occur.
Clean Aviation aims at maturing and demonstrating all critical technologies required to power
21

hydrogen-powered aircraft, such as the liquid hydrogen (LH2) storage systems, hydrogen distribution
systems, and hydrogen propulsion systems; ready for integration into these future hydrogen-powered
aircraft concepts.
Due to the specific constraints and opportunities of using hydrogen as a fuel, the aircraft integration of
these technologies may lead to new classes of aircraft with their own specific capabilities, besides the
current REG and SMR market segmentation. The demonstrations in the hydrogen-powered aircraft
pillar will also be dedicated to maturing the hydrogen technology integration for the different
hydrogen-powered aircraft concepts. Clean Aviation will assess hydrogen-powered aircraft concepts
based on two distinct propulsion solutions being either a hydrogen combustion (H2C) propulsion
system or a hydrogen fuel cell propulsion system (FCPS).
The first phase of the programme (up to 2026) is focused on the demonstration of all relevant H2
system architectures required to enable a future hydrogen powered aircraft: liquid hydrogen storage
on-board, fuel distribution systems, fuel-cell-based propulsion drive trains, and direct combustion of
hydrogen in a gas turbine-based engine. This includes the selection and validation of the most suitable
system concepts, to demonstrate the required performance, lifetime, costs, and safety. Beyond that,
the integration of these systems requires a deep understanding of operational, maintenance, and
certification aspects. To leverage the benefits of hydrogen propulsion, the high-level requirements of
potential aircraft platforms are considered from the beginning.
Clean Aviation projects selected in the first phase of the programme and contributing to the
development of disruptive technologies to enable hydrogen-powered aircraft include CAVENDISH,
TROPHY and HYDEA, developing hydrogen-burn turbine demonstrators; NEWBORN, FAME and HEROPS
developing next generation of hydrogen fuel cells-based powertrain; H2ELIOS, developing an innovative
light weight foam based hydrogen tank; FLHYing-Tank, developing hydrogen light-weight tank
demonstrator and HyPoTraDE, developing hydrogen fuel cell electric powertrain demonstrator.
Hydrogen systems are developed for different propulsion architectures (fuel cell or H2-burn
architectures) as well as aircraft sizes (commuter, regional, and short/medium range). Building on this,
radical short and medium range aircraft are expected to benefit from storage and feed system
architectures used to exploit hydrogen technology, paving the way for larger and longer-range
applications.
While the results of the phase 1 studies confirmed the feasibility of the different systems enabling the
use of hydrogen as a non-drop-in fuel, progress in the hydrogen production and infrastructure
ecosystem development - expected to occur outside the programme, has been slower than expected.
This has affected the TROPHY and FLHYing-Tank projects, for which de-scoping and termination have
since been implemented. Nevertheless, FLHYing-Tank was able to contribute to low TRL maturation
objectives. As a consequence of these delays and the slower progress,. , the scope for the second phase
of the programme has been revised at programme level in order to focus on improving the critical
components and sub-system performance, as needed to demonstrate the viability of the hydrogen-
powered aircraft concepts.
In the second phase of the programme, a second design iteration of the critical systems will be
performed, supporting both the fuel cell based propulsion aircraft concept and a hydrogen combustion

1. Objectives
NEWBORN focuses on development and demonstration of the TRL 4 ground demonstrator of the
overall propulsion system using fuel cells technology. The consortium plans to investigate the
technology for CS-23 19-pax commuter aircraft with a total system take-off power of approximately 2

demonstrate a self-regulating, load-bearing cryogenic tank with high gravimetric index and minimal
boil-off, but, as reflected in a project amendment, switched to using an existing LH2 cryotank to de-risk

conversion, propulsion systems, and the next generation microtube heat exchangers, along with an

Reference: 101102003
1. Objectives
The H2ELIOS project will develop an innovative and effective lightweight Liquid Hydrogen (LH2) storage
system for aircraft, duly supported by component and subsystem ground tests at appropriate scale at
project completion Initially, H2ELIOS focused on an LH2 storage concept integral to the fuselage.
Following valuable recommendations from EASA, the project pivoted to a non-integral LH2 storage
concept. This change facilitates and de-risks the initial certification roadmap towards a future product.
H2ELIOS will provide a feasible and novel low-pressure double-layer composite tank-based system.
General effectiveness will be assessed in terms of high gravimetric performance and ease of integration
within the aircraft structure. H2ELIOS proposes an innovative and disruptive LH2 storage solution that
adapts to the dormancy needs of the aircraft typical use while minimizes the weight devoted to the
tank. This concept will be supported by the latest evolutions of innovative methods and technologies
in terms of multidisciplinary design development, manufacturing processes and means of compliance,
and shall be demonstrated with a full-scale demonstrator on ground. The original target of TRL5 has
been revised considering delayed readiness of novel materials and manufacturing methods, as
reflected in a project amendment. Nevertheless, the project ambition to full-scale ground test
demonstration is maintained, achieving a TRL4 within H2elios scope, paving the way for possible Phase
2 activity.

• HyPoTraDe (Hydrogen Fuel Cell Electric Power Train Demonstration) - Project Reference:
101101998
1. Objectives
HyPoTraDe focuses on developing and testing a modular 500 kW fuel cell battery hybrid powertrain,
scalable up to the MW class. It also explores utilising the fuel cell's residual heat to enhance system
efficiency and tests the powertrain under flight-relevant conditions (with altitudes up to 25,000 ft).
Given the important of safety in aviation, the potential failures of the powertrain will be analysed, and
the necessary mitigations will be validated in the test campaign.
The project will create a digital twin validated by test data, enabling accurate performance predictions
for future scaled powertrains. Its distinctive feature, modularity, will enable the various components to
be interchanged with other validated subsystems, thus paving the way to digital certification process.
The key impact of HyPoTraDe lies in fast-track characterisation of fuel cell powertrain architectures,
providing the members of the CAJU with a comprehensive understanding of the operational
characteristics of modular, fuel cell - battery hybrid-electric, distributed electric propulsion powertrain
architectures. Thus, the results of the project will contribute to fulfilling the ambitious goals of the
programme, including regional and short-range hydrogen-powered aircraft with EIS in 2035 to meet
EU’s climate neutrality targets by 2050.

distribution system, propulsive loads including the electric motors, inverters and propellers, emulated aircraft
non-propulsive loads, and also a complex thermal management system which will be connected to all
abovementioned subsystems. The test campaign will demonstrate the feasibility of a system architecture
capable of increasing system efficiency by reusing residual thermal power of the fuel cell systems and will allow
for the validation of a modular digital twin suitable for a future digital certification process, and for failure mode
mitigation strategies in emulated test flights.

The project was launched with the aim to support the development of H2C (Hydrogen Combustion)
propulsion systems compatible with an Entry Into Service of a zero-CO low-emission aircraft in 2035.

future flight test activities. Consistently with the update of the Hydrogen Combustion (H2C)

• HEROPS (Hydrogen-Electric Zero Emission Propulsion System) - Project Reference: 101140499
1. Objectives
HEROPS aims to introduce climate-neutral propulsion into regional aircraft by developing MTU’s Flying
Fuel Cell™ (FFC) propulsion system concept. This disruptive hydrogen-electric propulsion system uses
fuel cells (FC) as sole power source and a liquid hydrogen fuel system without the need for high-power
batteries. Integration of both the FC system and the electric propulsion unit into a compact engine
nacelle will ensure an efficient system at high power-to-weight ratio.
HEROPS targets to demonstrate a 1,2 MW propulsion system. The core module and all further sub-
systems will confirm scalability to the 2–4 MW power level through simulation and testing. All aviation-
native technologies will be matured against relevant certification requirements. HEROPS also includes
a wind tunnel test of the FFC wetted parts (propeller, nacelle outer surfaces and heat exchanger) to
prove aerodynamics and drag performance of the whole system at TRL5.
HEROPS paves the way for the overall programme to advance the FFC concept for integration and
demonstration on a regional aircraft and for commercial prototyping and prepare for entry into service.
It delivers key propulsion technologies to reach the European Green Deal’s objective of climate-neutral
aviation with 100% prevention of CO and NOx.

1. Objectives
Green hydrogen as a fuel offers the possibility to significantly reduce or even eliminate certain aircraft’s
greenhouse gas emissions. Its adoption in combination with fuel cells (FC) for propulsive power
generation has the potential to achieve no CO , no SOx and no NOx emissions en route. However, to

bring a fuel cell (FC) aircraft to the market, the most promising way is to develop the FC propulsion

requiring a co-creation approach of propulsion system and aircraft. FAME follows this approach by
collaborative R&D between partners involved in the development of all needed subsystems and the
engine integrator and aircraft design organisation, thereby ensuring an optimisation at all levels.
FAME focuses on developing a complete compact high-efficiency full electric propulsion system based

integrated into a megawatt-class FC propulsion system ground demonstrator, with a route to scale it
up to aircraft level. FAME’s overall objective is to show the feasibility of a multi-MW FC propulsion
system for HPA providing the basis for a future flight test of the system.

Impact Monitoring Framework of the Clean Aviation programme
Clean Aviation aims to integrate and demonstrate disruptive aircraft technological innovations to
decrease net emissions of greenhouse gases by no less than 30% by 2030, compared to 2020 state-of-
the-art technology, while paving the ground towards climate-neutral aviation by 2050. The Council
Regulation (EU) 2021/2085 assigned the additional task to the JU, of monitoring and assessing the
technological progress towards the achievement of its objectives, in line with the Strategic Research
and Innovation Agenda (SRIA).
This task, ensured by the Executive Director under the direct supervision of the Governing Board, covers
the monitoring and assessment of the Clean Aviation Work Programme activities emanating from the
calls for proposals that will implement the Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda, towards
achieving the general and specific objectives of Clean Aviation.
The independent impact monitoring of aviation research and innovation, in general, will be carried out
under the responsibility of the European Commission within its collaborative research programme in
order to contribute to the definition and impact assessments of future EU aviation policies to support
the EU position in ICAO, the evolution of EASA environmental certification requirements and reporting
framework (including the European Aviation Environmental Report), and to communicate the impact
of EU aviation research and relevant policies.
In Phase 1, the Clean Aviation aircraft integrator projects (SMR ACAP and HERA), supported by the
propulsion and system suppliers and their participants in projects (RTOs, academia and SMEs) are
responsible for providing aircraft performance predictions, including the environmental impact at
aircraft level against the Council Regulation (EU) 2021/2085 objectives. They are integrating all the
results stemming from different projects contributing to an aircraft concept (in one report) and provide
visualisations of the cumulated programme impacts as compared to the objectives set in the SRIA,
including interdependencies between technical, operational, and environmental dimensions.
62

This task follows a well-developed intervention logic with clear objectives and targeted impacts,
measurable expected outcomes, deliverables and milestones within a defined timeframe, as well as
adequate resources and portfolio of activities to match these.
Both a qualitative and quantitative objective setting will be performed through the definition and
selection of relevant aircraft concepts/configurations, versus a well-defined baseline (state-of-the-art
2020 reference aircraft) for comparable top-level aircraft requirements.
These overall aircraft concepts allow for a breakdown of the objectives into key subsystem areas
(propulsion system, wing, fuselage, etc.) and finally key technologies and demonstrators. This
breakdown enables the identification of the relevant Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) at each level,
likely to undergo an iterative process during Phase 1 of the programme, until convergence before the
start of Phase 2. The KPIs were defined using SMART criteria: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant,
and Time-bound.
At aircraft concept level, the high-level objective, as stated in the Council Regulation (EU) 2021/2085,
towards achieving at least 30% GHG net emissions reduction versus the State-of-the-Art 2020 were
translated into emissions and fuel burn reduction targets and/or aircraft energy efficiency targets when
new fuels such as hydrogen are considered. This will allow the alignment/reconciliation of the
objectives defined in the SRIA (in terms of CO emission targets per aircraft concepts or technologies -
2
without any effect of sustainable aviation fuel) with those defined in the Regulation (in terms of net
GHG emissions) once getting further scientific knowledge and inputs.
At key subsystem area level, those KPIs were translated into specific target performance parameters
required to realise a given concept, such as tailpipe emissions, efficiency and power density of an engine
or any power train configuration, aerodynamic (lift and drag, etc.) and weight/structural performance
of a wing configuration, as non-exhaustive examples.
In order to ensure measurable outcomes, each project will provide a specific deliverable to the aircraft
concept owners on a yearly basis, as well as a final impact/performance assessment at completion,
including a TRL assessment.
In Phase 1, aircraft concept projects (SMR ACAP and HERA as aircraft integrators) performed a
consolidated assessment of the performance and maturity progress at aircraft level based on the
individual technology assessments stemming from the different linked projects contributing to an
aircraft concept. This assessment will be updated on a yearly basis to monitor the evolution of the
aircraft concept performance, based on the updated inputs received from other projects.
This information flow was complemented by the well-established Programme Management and
Reporting activities, such as the Annual and Periodic Reviews by independent experts and the Annual
Activity Report with the Programme KPIs.
The CAJU follow up these tasks and the associated deliverables within the frame of the Work
Programme activities. The Executive Director ensures the programme’s monitoring and assessment of
the progress compared to relevant impact indicators and the Joint Undertaking’s specific objectives,
under the supervision of the Governing Board and in coordination with advisory bodies where relevant
(consultations by the Scientific Advisory Board and States Representatives Group), and in accordance
with monitoring and evaluation principles set out in the Council Regulation (EU) 2021/2085.

2.4.1 Calls for Proposals
The Clean Aviation Calls for Proposals are open to all. Members as well as non-members of the CAJU
are equally invited to participate in these calls.
The Work Programme and Budget 2026-2027 covers:
- the execution of Phase 1 through the implementation, monitoring and assessment of Innovation
Actions and Coordination and Support Actions selected from the two Calls for Proposals launched
under the Work Programme 2022 and 2023 covering activities needed in the SMR, HER and HPA

- the execution of Phase 2 through the implementation, monitoring and assessment of Innovation

as Fast-Track Activities (FTAs)
- the preparation of Phase 2 Calls for Proposals in 2026 and 2027, followed by the evaluation and

The proposed strategy is to launch one call per year in early 2026 (Call 4) and early 2027 (Call 5) as part
of the total funding available for Phase 2 (approximately €930 million).
The Calls will address the integration and demonstration of technological innovations around the Clean
Aviation targeted aircraft concepts described in the SRIA. They will also include FTAs to bring not only
more flexibility at the level of the call and the grant agreement preparation but also create additional
opportunities for RTOs, academia and SMEs to enable them to bring technical competences and
contribution to the Programme.
Whereas Call 4 targets smaller projects in terms of budget and technical complexity, the Call 5 aims to
address mainly demonstration activities contributing to the market uptake of the generated disruptive
technologies and innovative solutions. Call 4 focuses on the Fast Track Activities (FTAs) contributing to
the projects resulting from Call 4 by de-risking alternative, additional technologies and technical
solutions that may contribute to the 2035 EIS and to follow a quicker implementation path. FTAs on de-

including from universities, research centres, and SMEs.

The Governance of the Clean Aviation Joint Undertaking is ensured by the Governing Board. Other
bodies are:
- the Executive Director;
- the Technical Committee;
- the Clean Aviation Scientific Advisory Body;
- the States Representatives Group.
The Governing Board (GB) gathers the Commission’s representatives [2] and those of the private
members [15], with the Commission holding 50% of the voting rights. Decisions are taken by a majority
of at least 75% of all votes during its ordinary meetings or by written procedure. The Governing Board
has the overall responsibility for the strategic orientation and the operations and supervises the
implementation of its activities. Some of the GB’s annual tasks include:
- assessment of applications for membership;
- adoption of annual budget including the staff establishment plan;
- providing guidance to and monitoring the performance of the Executive Director;
- adoption of the work programme;
- approval of the annual activity report, including the corresponding expenditure;
- approval of the list of actions to be funded etc.;
- adopt by the end of 2023 a plan for the phasing-out of the Joint Undertaking from Horizon
Europe funding upon recommendation of the Executive Director.
The Executive Director is the legal representative of the Clean Aviation Joint Undertaking. They are the
chief executive responsible for the day-to-day management of the Joint Undertaking, in accordance
with the decisions of the Governing Board. The Executive Director is in charge of the implementation
of the work programme with the support of the Programme Office. The Executive Director is supported
by four heads of unit (HoU): the Programme Development and Communications HoU, Project
Management HoU, the Governance HoU and the Administration and Finance HoU.
The specific tasks of the Executive Director are further described in Article 19 of the SBA. Following an
open and transparent selection procedure Axel Krein was appointed Executive Director of the Clean Sky
2 JU (predecessor of the Clean Aviation JU) on 1 February 2019 for a term of three years. His mandate

been adapted where necessary to the CAJU work environment. The continuous self-assessment by the

The CAJU internal control assessment takes into consideration the application of the internal control
principles, monitoring indicators, staff survey, compliance documentation, results of controls
throughout the reporting year, exception reports, specific control weaknesses or risks identified,
reports and recommendations received from the JU’s auditors and other reliable sources.
The results of the assessment of internal controls are presented periodically to the staff to raise
awareness and ensure a good understating of the JU’s internal control system.
Based on the conclusions of the periodic JU internal control assessment, the CAJU management
implements a continuous improvement plan, with clear milestones and actions, to ensure efficiency in
the JU activities and a well-functioning internal control system, enabling adequate JU objectives
monitoring and achievement.

2.7.3 Ex-ante and ex-post controls
Ex-ante controls:
During the period 2026-2027, the administration and finance unit and the operational unit will continue

will follow a risk-based monitoring approach, ensuring sound financial management, which will
contribute to further reducing the risk of incompliance, failing projects and/or loss of funding in the
final stage of the CA programme, in line with the Horizon Europe Control Strategy.
These activities will be conducted in a timely manner and monitored through the KPIs, in particular, for

Ex-post controls:
The Ex-post audit (EPA) process represents a significant element of the internal control system of the

- To ensure the legality and regularity of the validation of cost claims performed by the CAJU’s
management;
- To provide an adequate indication on the effectiveness of the related ex-ante controls;
- To provide the basis for corrective and recovery activities, if necessary
The ex-post audits take place in accordance with the HE Control and ex-post audit strategies and the

The ex-post audit activities for EU Framework Programmes for Research and Innovation (R&I) grants

The control objective, similar to previous programmes, is to keep the control system adapted to the

2.7.4 Risk management Strategy
As one major element of its Internal Control Framework, CAJU applies risk management through a
range of dedicated processes covering all areas of the CAJU’s activities.
The risk management strategy of the CAJU aims at improving the oversight for the CAJU’s Governing
Board and management regarding the potential threats for implementing the CAJU’s strategy, including
the dedicated process for an independent impact monitoring of the Clean Aviation programme and
aviation research and innovation in general.
In addition, risks are considered for driving the CAJU’s performance, leading to a contribution of the
risk management process towards understanding the impact of risks on performance and improving
the setting of performance targets.
Finally, the CAJU risk management also aims at reducing the extent of irregularities and fraud.
The complexity of the CAJU activities, with the involvement of many stakeholders participating in the
execution of the programmes requires assessing and managing risks at the different levels of activity:
• Joint Undertaking organisational level;
• Programme level;
• Thrusts and technology areas covered by the CA WP objectives and performances

and description of the mitigating activities. With respect to the methodology used, the CAJU follows
the Impact/Likelihood concept:
The impact is the potential consequence on the achievement of the set objectives, should the potential
event materialise. The likelihood reflects the probability of occurrence, considering the mitigating
actions which are planned or have been taken.
